lines.text: Next they found an island full of wild goats, and across a narrow stretch of water, the land of the Cyclopes.
These were giant shepherds with a single eye in the middle of the forehead.
They had no laws and no ships, and they had no fear of the gods at all.
The sensible thing was to leave them alone. Odysseus wanted to see them, though.
He wanted to know who they were and whether they'd give him gifts, the way a host was supposed to.
So he took twelve men and a skin of very strong wine and climbed to a cave above the sea.
The cave was full: cheeses stacked on racks, pens crowded with lambs and kids, buckets of milk.
The owner was out with his flock.
His men begged him to grab the cheese and a few lambs and run.
Odysseus said no. He wanted to meet him.
At evening the owner came home.
His name was Polyphemus, and he was a son of Poseidon, god of the sea.
He drove his flock inside, picked up a stone that twenty-two wagons couldn't have shifted, and closed the door of the cave with it.
Then he lit a fire, and he saw them.
Odysseus stepped forward and spoke the way a guest is supposed to.
We're Greeks, on our way home from Troy, he said. The gods protect travellers, and we ask for your hospitality.
The Cyclops laughed at him. We don't care about your gods, he said. We're stronger than they are.
Then he grabbed two of the men, smashed them against the floor like puppies, and ate them, bones and all.
He washed them down with milk, lay down among his sheep, and went to sleep.
Odysseus drew his sword. He could have killed him right there.
But then they'd all die in that cave anyway, because no man alive could move the stone in the doorway.
So they waited.
In the morning the Cyclops ate two more men for breakfast, took his flock out, and rolled the stone back into place behind him.
Lying in the cave was a club of green olive wood, as long as a ship's mast.
Odysseus cut off a length of it, sharpened one end, hardened the point in the fire, and hid it under the dung.
That evening the Cyclops came home and ate two more men, and Odysseus walked right up to him holding a bowl of the dark wine.
Here, Cyclops, he said. Have a drink, after your dinner of men.
The Cyclops drank it and loved it. He asked for another, and then a third.
And then, very kindly, he asked: what's your name, stranger? I'd like to give you a present.
My name, said Odysseus, is Nobody.
Then here's your present, Nobody, the Cyclops said. I'll eat you last.
And he fell over backwards, drunk, and started snoring.
They pushed the stake into the coals until it glowed.
Four men lifted it with Odysseus and drove it into the eye,
and Odysseus leaned his weight on it and twisted, the way a shipwright works a drill.
The Cyclops screamed so loudly the whole mountain rang.
His neighbours came running and shouted through the stone: Polyphemus, what's wrong? Is somebody killing you?
And from inside, he roared back: Nobody is killing me!
Well, they said, if nobody's hurting you, it must be a sickness sent by the gods. You'd better pray to your father. And they went home.
In the morning the blind giant rolled the stone aside and sat in the doorway with his hands out, feeling every sheep that went past.
Odysseus had tied his men under the bellies of the rams, three rams to each man.
For himself he took the biggest ram of the flock and hung underneath it, gripping the wool, and the giant's hands passed right over his back.
They ran for the ships, and they got away.
And this is the moment Odysseus threw everything away.
As the ship pulled out, he stood up and shouted back at the island.
Cyclops! If anyone asks who blinded you, tell them it wasn't Nobody.
It was Odysseus, sacker of cities, son of Laertes, from Ithaca!
His men begged him to shut up.
The giant tore off the top of a hill and threw it at the sound of his voice, and the wave nearly carried the ship back onto the beach.
But Odysseus wanted the credit. He'd won with a fake name, and he couldn't stand nobody knowing his real one.
Now the Cyclops knew exactly who to curse. He lifted his hands to the sea and prayed to his father:
Poseidon, if I'm really your son, never let Odysseus reach home.
Or if he has to get there, let him get there late, and alone, on somebody else's ship, and let him find trouble in his house.
And Poseidon heard him.
